specPoints.text: use the law of reflection (the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection)
draw ray diagrams to illustrate reflection and refraction
explain that all waves can be reflected and refracted

primer.text: Reflection and refraction are the two doors every wave meets at a boundary: one turns it back, the other bends it onward. You can already name both behaviours for light and sound; this lesson adds the measuring law for reflection and the drawing rules that turn those laws into full-mark ray diagrams.

lessons.title: Reflection & the law of reflection
lessons.opening: Reflection happens when a wave meets the boundary between two media and stays in the one it came from, like a tree mirrored in still water. The law that governs it is symmetrical: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal, the line at right angles to the boundary.
keyPoints: All waves, transverse or longitudinal, can be reflected and refracted.
Reflection keeps the wave in its original medium at the boundary.
The law of reflection states that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
Both angles are measured between the ray and the normal.
The normal is the line at ninety degrees to the boundary surface.

low.restatement: At a reflecting boundary the wave bounces back into its own medium, and the angle it arrived at, measured from the normal, equals the angle it leaves at.
low.analogy: A ball thrown at a wall straight-on comes straight back; thrown at a slant it leaves at the same slant, mirrored.
low.examPointer: Always draw and label the normal first; angles measured from the boundary itself score zero.

medium.restatement: The equality of the two angles is the reversible symmetry of the path: send a ray along the reflected direction and it retraces the incident one, which is why mirror layouts in periscopes and reflectors work in both directions.
medium.analogy: A corridor with one mirrored wall: walk any route in and the mirror sends you out along the exact mirror twin of your path.
medium.examPointer: For the mark, quote i = r in words as well as symbols, and name both angles from the normal.

check.stem: Reflection happens when a wave arrives at a boundary and:

options.text: passes into the new medium and bends
options.explanation: That describes refraction.

options.text: stays in the original medium, bouncing back
options.explanation: Reflected waves do not cross into the second medium.
The wave continues, redirected.
Dispersion is a separate effect.

check.stem: The law of reflection states that:

options.text: angle of incidence = angle of refraction
options.explanation: That confuses reflection with refraction.

options.text: angle of incidence is twice the angle of reflection
options.explanation: No doubling exists in the law.

options.text: angle of incidence = angle of reflection
options.explanation: That equality is the law, both angles from the normal.

options.text: the angles add to ninety degrees
options.explanation: No fixed sum is part of the law.

check.stem: Angles of incidence and reflection are measured between the ray and:

options.explanation: Measuring from the surface is the classic error.
The incident ray cannot measure its own angle.
Wavefronts are drawing aids, not angle references.
The normal is the reference line for all such angles.

check.stem: A ray strikes a plane mirror at 35 degrees from the normal. It leaves at:

options.text: 35 degrees from the normal on the other side
options.explanation: The reflection angle equals the incidence angle.
That subtracts from ninety unnecessarily.
No doubling applies.

options.text: 35 degrees measured from the mirror surface
options.explanation: Angles are quoted from the normal, not the surface.
Sound and water waves reflect too.
Longitudinal waves reflect as echoes.
Reflection is universal across the wave families.

options.text: none, it is a light-only effect
options.explanation: The spec statement is explicitly about all waves.

check.stem: State the law of reflection in words.
check.modelAnswer: The incidence angle equals the reflection angle, both measured from the normal.
The normal is the construction line at right angles (ninety degrees) to the boundary from which angles are measured.

check.stem: Explain why measuring reflection angles from the mirror surface instead of the normal gives the wrong comparison.
check.modelAnswer: The law compares angles defined from the normal, so measuring from the surface gives each angle as its complement to ninety degrees; two unequal incidence and reflection angles could then appear equal, hiding the true geometry.

check.stem: A tree stands by a calm lake and its image appears below it in the water. Name the effect and state the equality that governs each ray involved.
check.modelAnswer: The image is produced by reflection at the water surface; every ray obeys the law of reflection, leaving at an angle from the normal equal to the angle at which it arrived.

lessons.title: Ray diagrams & refraction
lessons.opening: Ray diagrams reduce waves to arrowed lines, incident arrows pointing at the boundary and reflected arrows pointing away. Refraction adds a bend whose direction follows optical density: into a denser medium the ray bends towards the normal, out of one it bends away, and along the normal it does not bend at all.
keyPoints: An incident ray is drawn with its arrow pointing towards the boundary.
A reflected ray is drawn with its arrow pointing away from the boundary.
Entering a denser medium, light bends towards the normal.
Leaving a denser medium, light bends away from the normal.
Speed and wavelength change during refraction but frequency does not.

low.restatement: Ray diagrams use straight arrowed lines: into denser media the bend is towards the normal, out of them it is away, and frequency never changes even though speed and wavelength do.
low.analogy: A trolley rolling from pavement onto mud veers towards the normal as its wheels slow on the near side.
low.examPointer: Remember the paired phrase: enters towards, leaves away; arrows on every ray are compulsory.

medium.restatement: The bend is the geometry of a speed change: the wavefront edge that arrives first slows first, rotating the front, which also explains why the frequency survives unchanged while wavelength rescales with speed.
medium.analogy: A car pair turning as one wheel hits gravel before the other: the axle pivots without the engine changing its rhythm.
medium.examPointer: The unchanged-frequency argument via colour is the classic explanation mark: light does not change colour on refracting.

check.stem: On a ray diagram, the arrow of the incident ray points:

options.explanation: That is the reflected ray convention.
Incident rays travel into the boundary.
No convention points rays along the surface here.
Each ray carries one direction arrow.

check.stem: Light passes from air into glass. The refracted ray bends:

options.explanation: That is the glass-to-air direction.
No bending happens only along the normal.
That would be reflection, not refraction.
Into the denser medium the ray bends towards the normal.

check.stem: Light leaves the glass block back into air. The emerging ray bends:

options.explanation: Into the less dense medium the ray bends away from the normal.
That is the air-to-glass direction.
That special case is not the general exit behaviour.
Rays bend linearly at flat boundaries.

options.text: frequency and speed, but not wavelength
options.explanation: Frequency is the survivor; wavelength follows speed.
Frequency never changes on refraction.

options.text: speed and wavelength, but not frequency
options.explanation: The medium changes the speed and the wavelength rescales with it.
A speed change is the cause of the bending.

check.stem: A ray hits a boundary exactly along the normal. It:

options.explanation: It is already on the normal; there is nothing to bend towards.
Partial reflection may occur, but the listed behaviour is straight-through transmission.
The wave continues into the new medium.
Along the normal there is no direction change on refraction.

check.stem: State the bending rule for light entering a denser medium.
State what happens to the frequency of light during refraction.
Explain why a pencil standing in a glass of water looks bent at the surface.
check.modelAnswer: Light from the underwater part leaves the water and bends away from the normal into the air, so the rays reaching your eye come from a shifted apparent direction and the pencil appears bent at the boundary.

check.stem: A ray diagram must show a beam travelling air-to-glass-to-air through a rectangular block. Sketch description: state the bend at each boundary and the arrow directions.
check.modelAnswer: At the air-to-glass face the ray bends towards the normal as it enters; at the glass-to-air face it bends away from the normal as it leaves; the incident arrow points at the first boundary and the emerging arrow points away from the block on the far side.

glossary.definition: A material that transmits light; more than one is called media.
The construction line at right angles to a boundary from which angles are measured.
The angle between the incoming ray and the normal.
The angle between the outgoing reflected ray and the normal.
A measure of how much a material slows light passing through it.
